The sculpture is a seated walnut-wood Virgin, still carrying traces of its original gilding and polychrome, measuring 54 centimeters tall and holding the figure of the Christ Child—though she’s missing both forearms.
Small enough to wrap in a blanket, valuable enough to disappear into the antiques trade for decades, that combination made her exactly Erik’s type.

A veritable manifestation of the fictional Arsène Lupin, Van den Berghe (1940–2020) robbed churches and monasteries across sparsely populated parts of his adopted country of Spain and elsewhere in Europe.
Thousands of crimes have been attributed to him, much of it involving medieval sacred art.

“We are lucky, which does not always happen, that [the owner] understood that it was the virgin that Erick the Belgian stole from San Pedro de Meoz and they immediately wanted to return her.

source_passages: Home All News World Roman Glass Among the Silk Road Treasures Unearthed in Nomadic Noble’s Tomb An aerial view of the tomb – credit National Museum of Korea The legendary character of the Silk Road was in full focus recently in Mongolia, where excavations of a nomad’s tomb unearthed objects all the way from Classical Rome.

The shards of a glass cup from Rome – credit National Museum of Korea In addition to a cup made from Roman glass, a gourd-shaped silver and crystal pendant, likely used to adorn a horse’s harness, closely resembles accessories found in tombs on the Korean Peninsula that date to the same period.

Excavations on Tomb 160 found 413 artifacts, including precious metals and stones, and an entire lacquered chariot, indicating that whoever was interred there likely occupied the highest social position.

fact_checks.sentence: Cette sépulture, mesurant près de 240 pieds de long, témoigne de la place centrale des nomades dans un réseau d’échanges s’étendant de Rome à la Corée, en passant par la Chine.
source_passages: Home All News World Roman Glass Among the Silk Road Treasures Unearthed in Nomadic Noble’s Tomb An aerial view of the tomb – credit National Museum of Korea The legendary character of the Silk Road was in full focus recently in Mongolia, where excavations of a nomad’s tomb unearthed objects all the way from Classical Rome.
The discoveries highlight the Xiongnu’s role in a vast exchange network that linked these progenitors of the conquering Mongols to the Roman Empire, Han China, and the Korean Peninsula.
A need to secure horses to wage war on the Xiongnu required a stable route to Central Asia, which saw the establishment of Chinese control over the Gansu Corridor.

fact_checks.sentence: Les fouilles, menées en collaboration entre institutions mongoles et coréennes, ont aussi mis au jour un chars laqué et plusieurs pièces de jade manifestant des influences croisées entre Han et Xiongnu.
source_passages: NOMAD NEWS: Asiatic Wild Ass Returns to Eastern Mongolia After 65-year Isolation from Landscape Fencing The tomb was excavated over a 4-year period by a collaborative team from the National Museum of Korea, the Institute of Archaeology at the Mongolian Academy of Sciences, and the National Museum of Mongolia.

Excavations on Tomb 160 found 413 artifacts, including precious metals and stones, and an entire lacquered chariot, indicating that whoever was interred there likely occupied the highest social position.
Fifteen jade pieces, modeled after Han funerary goods but bearing their own distinct designs, were also found.

fact_checks.sentence: Ces trouvailles précisent les transformations sociales et les conflits qui ont marqué la fin de l’empire Xiongnu, tout en enrichissant la connaissance des interactions précoces entre ces civilisations.
source_passages: This contrasts with deeper tombs in central Mongolia, suggesting changes in Xiongnu society during the late first and second centuries CE, a period when the empire was declining due to internal conflicts and pressure from the Han military.
This information will help further understand the Xiongnu’s social structure and trade networks.
The National Museum of Korea stated that the excavation demonstrates the Xiongnu’s links to a broad exchange network stretching from Rome to the Korean Peninsula.

fact_checks.sentence: Les fossiles résultent de traces ou restes d'anciens organismes conservés dans des roches sédimentaires, que ce soit par minéralisation ou moulages naturels.
source_passages: Un fossile (du latin fossilis, « tiré de la terre », adjectif dérivé du verbe fodere, « fouir ») est la trace plus ou moins minéralisée d'un ancien organisme vivant ou de son activité passée, ou bien son simple moulage, conservés dans une roche sédimentaire.

Il peut s'agir de restes plus ou moins bien conservés de l'organisme lui-même (ossements, dents, feuilles, mycélium, biofilm, etc.) ou d'empreintes qu'il a laissées (empreintes de pas, de peau ou d’autres téguments), de moulages externes naturels (dans de l’ambre, par exemple), de terriers, de stromatolithes, de coprolithes, etc.
